gaps.note: MegaETH. The high-throughput unit cleared assumption A1 with the statement that the KeylessDeploy sandbox has its own journal and cannot see the parent's transient storage. That property alone is the dangerous shape named in the settlement unit's high lead: a nested run with an empty transient map whose storage and balance changes are merged back would let a caller sync a token outside, pay, settle and mint a claim inside, and settle again outside for the same tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364, 322-329). Critic check on 2026-11-22, read only: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/system/intercept.rs returns no interception when ctx.is_inside_sandbox() is true or depth is nonzero (lines 298 to 303), and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/megaeth-labs/mega-evm/main/crates/mega-evm/src/sandbox/mod.rs states that a call from a contract reaches the Solidity fallback and reverts with NotIntercepted. A sandbox therefore starts only as the first frame of a transaction, when the PoolManager has no transient state yet. The clearance stands for that reason and the recorded reason should be replaced. Still open: which mega-evm release and spec the mainnet sequencer runs, since both files were read on the main branch.

The special address sweeps on these chains are recorded as eth_call with the from field set to the PoolManager, or record no forwarding stub. In such a call tx.origin equals msg.sender and the caller looks like an account that sends a transaction. In a real take, sync or hook call the PoolManager is an inner frame and the origin is another account. The Ethereum, OP Stack, Monad and MegaETH units used a forwarding stub placed at the PoolManager address by state override, and the MegaETH unit saw L2StandardBridge accept the top-level call and reject the inner one. A target that requires its caller to be a contract, or that reads tx.origin for credit or refunds, would answer the two shapes differently. The eleven sweeps should be repeated with the stub for every target that did not revert and for every target that reverted with an origin or account type message.

Monad, Tempo and BNB Smart Chain. The opcode probes of both cycles ran as freshly created init code through eth_call. The Monad client runs bytecode in an interpreter first and switches to compiled native code once enough gas has been spent on that code (critic read of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/vm.cpp, lines 130 to 170), Tempo pins the evm2 JIT crate with unknown activation, and the BNB Smart Chain changelog records an opcode fusion interpreter with two consensus fixes whose location in the current client was not found. A probe made of new init code does not show how the deployed PoolManager bytecode runs under those paths. The liquidity unit reproduced modifyLiquidity amounts through the deployed PositionManager on 20 networks. No unit reproduced swap results through a deployed contract on any network, and Tempo was probed with one zero payment position only.

Tempo. The L3 profile lists balance writes and issuer roles and says nothing about gas, so assumption A9 is untested there. Critic reads on 2026-11-22: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tempoxyz/tempo/main/tips/tip-1000.md prices a write to an empty storage slot at 250,000 gas in place of 20,000 and sets the gas cap per transaction to 30,000,000. Block 50,314,865 on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz reports gasLimit 500,000,000 and mainBlockGeneralGasLimit 30,000,000. eth_feeHistory over the last 1,024 blocks returned a base fee of 600,000,000 in every block, and two block timestamps 3,745 blocks apart give 0.54 seconds per block. I did not establish whether PoolManager transactions count against the general limit, whether the base fee can move, or how a proposer orders transactions inside that limit.

HyperEVM. The A1 clearance and the system transaction rules rest on the archive client. The validator node is closed source. The unit could not confirm how HyperCore orders several system transactions in one block or how early an action must be sent to land ahead of signed transactions, and finding 1 of the unit has evidence marked inferred. The treasury designation rule behind F-020 and the new AQAv2 finding is still unread.

Elysium. Blocks are produced by a Conduit sequencer on a separate stack and only the RPC node, a locally built Nitro binary of unknown commit, was tested. The announced ArbOS upgrade with a HyperCore read precompile and an ElysiumCoreWriter predeploy is unscheduled on chain and lead L-001 is still open. More than 10,000 pools exist and their currencies and hooks were not enumerated.

Arc. Every source claim of both cycles was read on the arc-node main branch while the endpoint reports arc/v1. Whether Zero8 is active, and whether mainnet contains the ruint correction of v0.8.0 that concerns shift and overflow handling, is unknown. The pool math depends on those operations.

OP Mainnet. The endpoint reports op-reth/v0.0.0-dev-unknown. The source reading for this chain was taken from the commit that Unichain, Ink and Soneium report. The largest OP Stack deployment by value therefore has no client reading of its own.

Zora, Ink, Soneium and World Chain. The four L3 profiles repeat one sentence about the WETH predeploy, and the World Chain L3 profile cites no source at all. No unit listed the tokens these four PoolManagers hold or classified them for rebasing balances, second entry points or issuer controls. The cycle 1 critic raised the same point for three of them.

World Chain. The unit states that the parallel validation path for flashblocks with block access lists was not read to the end. That path decides whether each transaction runs on its own journal with a clean transient map.
Polygon. The unit states that the merge step of the BlockSTM executor was not read line by line. The clearance of A1 for parallel execution rests on the serial message path.

Unichain. The predeploy of 24,050 bytes is still assumed to behave like src/. The owner has ruled out a comparison of code copies. A behaviour test through eth_call with a caller contract placed by state override compares no code and was not tried: the outcomes of sync, settle with and without value after a token sync, settleFor, take, clear, mint and burn can be checked against src/PoolManager.sol line by line.

BNB Smart Chain and Tempo. Jenner and T14 both activate on 2026-12-08. Today the CAS20 address range, 0x70 and the ConfigurableAccount address 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 answer every call shape with success and empty data, as accounts without code do, so a take that names them debits the caller and moves nothing (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). The sweeps on both chains describe the state before the forks and expire on that date.

Seven units wrote the same open lead: list the currencies of all initialized pools from an indexer and classify them. The public endpoints limit eth_getLogs, so every unit sampled a token list. The samples found tokens whose balance changes without a transfer on five chains (AMPL and stETH on Ethereum, aTokens on Arbitrum One and MegaETH, USD+ on Base, stHYPE on HyperEVM). The full lists are missing on every chain.

titles: A native payout sent to L2ToL1MessagePasser, an ERC-4337 EntryPoint or the L1BlockNumber predeploy is booked to the PoolManager's own address and is lost to the caller
A native payout sent to a withdrawal predeploy, a fee vault, an EntryPoint or a Celo core contract is lost to the caller on Celo and X Layer
A payout sent to an EntryPoint, a precompile address or a protocol custody address is lost to the caller on Arc and Tempo
Three more recipients on HyperEVM accept a PoolManager payout and strand it: the L1 block number precompile, the ERC-4337 EntryPoints and a system address reached through the stHYPE contract
A payout sent to a HyperCore bridge address is credited to the PoolManager's HyperCore account and cannot be recovered
duplicates.note: One hazard on twelve chains. The caller who names the recipient is the only party that loses, as each verifier wrote. The four new entries carry actor unprivileged with effect freeze or degrade, which reads as an in-scope item. Merge them into F-021 as one low finding about recipient choice, and record for Ethereum, Monad, MegaETH, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche and the Arbitrum family, where the same behaviour was filed under cleared, that it is the same item.

Role holders on GHO, syrupUSDC, apxUSD, shMON and mUSD can pause, burn, move or replace balances that the Monad PoolManager holds
A pause of the USDC token on Arc stops the ERC-20 face and leaves native transfers open over the same PoolManager balance
Elysium USDC is a bridge representation whose backing on HyperEVM sits at one address that the issuer can block
One issuer blocklist entry on the PoolManager address freezes or wipes a stablecoin for every pool
duplicates.note: Same issuer control hazard as F-011, F-015, F-019, F-028 and F-032, now reported for Arbitrum One, Monad, Arc and Elysium. Keep one finding with a per chain token table. The Arc pause variant and the Elysium backing variant add a second step and should stay as named variants.

Polygon system token at 0x1010 mirrors the PoolManager native balance and cannot be paid out by take
Cleared: Faces, tokens with more than one entry point: SNX on OP Mainnet is reachable at the proxy and at its target
Cleared: Faces on Celo: the CELO token proxy, its implementation address, the four fee currency adapters
Cleared: Faces, native asset with the read only LegacyERC20ETH view

An address that answers balanceOf with a balance the PoolManager holds under another id and rejects transfer is a low finding on Arc and Polygon and a cleared item on OP Mainnet, Zora and Celo. The behaviour and the consequence are the same on all five: a credit under the mirror id needs a real payment and can never be taken out. Record it once, with one rule for the status.

Rebasing stETH held by the PoolManager gains and loses balance outside pool accounting
Any account can book a balance increase it triggers at the PoolManager as its own payment, and EIP-7702 removes the origin check that guards Ampleforth's public rebase
stHYPE and wstHYPE are two currency ids over one share balance, so a loss in the rebasing face is paid from the shares of pools in the other face
Cleared: Aave aTokens and other yield tokens at the MegaETH PoolManager

The Arbitrum One and MegaETH entries are the passive case and the HyperEVM entry adds two ids over one balance. The units also disagree on a fact that decides the active case for aTokens: the Arbitrum One unit says the whole flash loan premium goes to the protocol, while the Ethereum unit says premiums raise the supplier index inside the transaction. Both can be true per deployment and each chain should state which holds.

Cleared (cycle 1): tick spacing bounds, bitmap arithmetic, the liquidity cap per tick and overflow of in range liquidity

X Layer block builder can exclude PoolManager transactions through a rule driven risk control filter, which leaves L1 deposits as the exit
Operator transaction filtering on Robinhood Chain can fail any exit from the PoolManager, including force-included ones
duplicates.note: The new X Layer finding removes the mitigation that F-024 names, so F-024 should be updated in place and its severity aligned with F-001, which describes the same end state on Robinhood Chain.

The MRB hard fork raised the price of seven precompiles by 5 to 40 times, which can push a hook past the 3,000,000 gas fast block
duplicates.note: Both rest on the 3,000,000 gas block of HyperEVM and assumption A9. The first has evidence marked inferred from repository snapshots. One measured gas figure for an empty bitmap word and for a tick crossing on the deployed contract settles the first and bounds the second.

HyperCore sends unsigned system transactions from addresses outside the system range, which moves ERC-20 balances without any call by the holder
duplicates.note: The two entries give different answers to who can cause a system transaction. The new one says an ordinary account that links a spot token can make the node call its contract at the top of a block. F-020 carries actor operator. They describe two sender classes and the state should say which system transactions an ordinary HyperCore account can cause and which need a validator vote.

titles: Cleared: A1 from the node source: does transient storage end with the transaction, and does the KeylessDeploy sandbox share it
Lead (settlement unit, high): does any execution feature run code inside a call in a context whose transient storage is separate from the caller's
duplicates.note: Contradiction between units, resolved by the critic check recorded under gaps for chain 4326. The sandbox is safe because it starts only at depth zero, and the cleared entry should say so.

titles: Lead: do the deployed routers and position managers call sync(address(0)) before a native settle (settlement verifier, all chains)
Lead: do the Universal Router and PositionManager on Arc call sync(address(0)) before a native settle
Lead: which tokens raise a holder's balance through a call that any account can make (Ethereum, OP Stack, established L1, HyperEVM, Monad, Arbitrum and X Layer units)
Lead: enumerate currency0 and currency1 from the Initialize events (HyperEVM, Monad, Elysium, Arbitrum One, Ethereum units)
duplicates.note: Three questions were each written by several units for their own chains. Each needs one method applied to all 21 chains: one read of the router source, one indexer query for pool currencies, and one classification pass over the result.

leads.question: For each chain, name every feature that runs caller-chosen code against live state with a transient storage map other than the one of the surrounding transaction: Tempo zone contracts and the T14 ConfigurableAccount, Base Transactions of type 0x79, Stylus host calls and retryable redeems on the Arbitrum family, coreReceiveWithData system transactions on HyperEVM, PBH bundles on World Chain, the fee currency calls on Celo, and any keyless deploy, simulation or sandbox precompile. For each one, can an ordinary contract start it from inside a call, does the inner run begin with an empty or a copied transient map, and are its storage and balance writes kept?
leads.why: This is the one chain property that turns the settlement code into a direct loss for every pool. sync needs no lock and keeps the reserves in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). If an inner run with an empty map can pay tokens in, settle and mint a claim (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364, 322-329) and its writes are kept, the outer settle credits the same tokens a second time. If the inner run starts from a copy and drops its transient writes, a take inside it leaves no debit (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The settlement unit raised the question and no network unit answered it except for MegaETH, where the critic found that the sandbox starts only at depth zero.

leads.question: On each client, is there any way for a call frame to carry a nonzero CALLVALUE while the caller's balance does not fall by the same amount in the same journal? Check the system caller rule (go-ethereum master and BNB Smart Chain master skip the balance check and the transfer when the caller is 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe, read by the critic at core/vm/evm.go lines 311 to 347 of bnb-chain/bsc; Bor v2.11.0 does not), deposit transactions with a mint field on the OP Stack chains including the custom gas token chains, retryable tickets and unsigned L1 messages on the Arbitrum family, gasless transactions on X Layer, the sandbox signer on MegaETH, system transactions on HyperEVM, and fee payer or sponsored transactions on Tempo and Arc. Which sender addresses reach those paths and can any of them enter contract code that an ordinary account chose?
leads.why: A native credit is msg.value and nothing else (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354). The code never compares it with a balance change, so a frame that reports value it did not pay receives a native credit for free and can take every native balance and, through pools, other tokens. Assumption A3 lists the unit of msg.value and the faces of the native asset and does not list this. The established L1 unit recorded the system caller rule on BNB Smart Chain with relevance none and no unit asked the question for the other clients.

leads.question: Does the source text satisfy every statement the repository makes about itself in the files no unit has replayed? Replay by reading or by transcription: test/libraries/TickMath.t.sol, SqrtPriceMath.t.sol, SwapMath.t.sol, FullMath.t.sol, BitMath.t.sol, UnsafeMath.t.sol, StateLibrary.t.sol and Lock.t.sol, test/types/Currency.t.sol (the transfer cases from line 122 on), test/Tick.t.sol, test/DynamicFees.t.sol, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol, test/SkipCallsTestHook.t.sol, test/PoolManager.swap.t.sol, test/Extsload.t.sol, test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.t.sol and the hook and initialize cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol. Then compare every NatSpec sentence in src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol, IProtocolFees.sol and IHooks.sol with the function it describes, and compare src/PoolManager.sol with the two other implementations of the same interface inside this repository, src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol and src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol, function by function.
leads.why: The owner states that this build carries a planted weakness and has ruled out comparison with other copies. The tests, the interface comments and the test doubles in this repository are then the only reference for intended behaviour. Cycle 1 found four places where the source departs from them (F-006), two of them in Pool.swap, and lead L-118 is still open with the files listed here unread. A fifth departure in a path that moves funds would be the planted item or would point at it.

leads.question: protocolFeeController is the zero address on these eleven chains. For each client, which frames can have msg.sender equal to address(0): the system calls of Tempo's block executor, HyperEVM system transactions whose sender the node accepts as any 20 bytes, the Celo fee currency debit and credit calls, Monad and MegaETH system senders, OP Stack upgrade deposits, and ArbOS internal transactions on Elysium? Can an ordinary account choose the target or the calldata of any of them?
leads.why: setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees accept any caller that equals the stored controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-36, 48). A caller that can appear as address(0) could set the protocol fee of every pool to the cap and withdraw what accrues. The cycle 1 critic recorded contradicting clearances on this point. Cycle 2 answered it for X Layer and Avalanche only.

leads.question: On which of these chains is EIP-7702 or a native batch transaction type active, so that code runs while msg.sender equals tx.origin, and which tokens held by the PoolManager there guard a public rebase, reward push or mint with that test? Start from the tokens already named: USD+ on Base, the aTokens on Arbitrum One and MegaETH, and any Ampleforth style token.
leads.why: The Ethereum unit confirmed that an ordinary account can call a guarded rebase from inside its own unlock callback and book the rise of balanceOf(PoolManager) as its payment (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). No other unit tested which chains share that account model. Where one balance is read under two ids, as the HyperEVM unit found for stHYPE and wstHYPE, a rise booked under the rebasing id also removes the yield of pools in the other id, so the answer decides how far the Ethereum finding reaches.

leads.question: Does a distributor that pays holders on a third party's call owe anything to the PoolManager address on any chain? Check the Merkl distributor, Compound style claim functions, and any airdrop contract with a claim for an arbitrary account, for each of the ten largest token holdings of each PoolManager. What does one claim pay, in which token, and is that token the currency of any pool?
leads.why: A claim that any account can trigger raises a token balance of the PoolManager inside the caller's transaction. With sync before and settle after, the caller is credited the whole amount (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-364). The PoolManager is among the largest holders of many tokens, so reward programs that pay by holding are likely to list it. The Ethereum unit checked three such triggers on mainnet and none on the other chains.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the PoolManager change state for the sender when the PoolManager sends a transfer of zero: a transfer cooldown per sender, a counter of transfers per block, a reward that is claimed to the sender, or a fee swap inside the token? The call costs nothing: take(token, anyRecipient, 0) inside an unlock.
leads.why: take with amount zero makes the PoolManager call transfer and owes nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 368-369). A token that limits how often one sender may transfer would let any account use up that limit in every block and so stop every payout of that token to all pools, with no role and no cost beyond gas. The verifier of the established L1 unit asked this for three chains only.

leads.question: Repeat the special address sweep with a forwarding stub placed at the PoolManager address by state override and a different account as transaction sender. For which targets does the answer to empty calldata with value, transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address) or a hook selector differ from the answer to a top-level call from the PoolManager address?
leads.why: See the gap entry. The real calls are inner frames (src/types/Currency.sol:48, 73, 94 and src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). A target that pays or credits the origin, or that accepts only contract callers, was tested in the one shape that cannot occur.

leads.question: Through the Quoter listed in state/networks.json for each chain, quote an exact input and an exact output swap that crosses at least three initialized ticks in the largest pool, in both directions, and compare the amounts with a transcription of src/libraries/Pool.sol, SwapMath.sol and SqrtPriceMath.sol run on the pool state read through extsload at the same block. Do all 21 networks agree to the last unit?
leads.why: This runs the deployed PoolManager bytecode through each node's own execution path, including the compiled path on Monad, the evm2 path on Tempo and the fused interpreter on BNB Smart Chain, which the init code probes do not reach. A network whose result differs by one unit in the swapper's favour would let pools pay out more than they hold.

leads.question: On Tempo a write to an empty slot costs 250,000 gas and one transaction may use 30,000,000. What does one swap step cost when it crosses an initialized tick whose two fee growth slots are written for the first time, how many such crossings fit in one transaction, and what does it cost an ordinary account to initialize that many ticks with dust positions around the price of the largest pool? Does a removal of liquidity ever write an empty slot?
leads.why: The L3 profile has no gas figure. At 500,000 gas for the two fee growth slots alone, about sixty first time crossings fill a transaction, so dust positions can force a large trade into many transactions (src/libraries/Pool.sol swap loop and tick crossing). Removal of liquidity touches two ticks and should stay possible, which the measurement would confirm.

leads.question: Do transactions that call the PoolManager on Tempo count against mainBlockGeneralGasLimit, which block 50,314,865 reports as 30,000,000 against a block gasLimit of 500,000,000? Is the base fee of 600,000,000 per gas fixed by the protocol, and does a proposer order transactions inside the general limit by tip or by arrival? What does it cost per day to fill the general limit of every block with cheap transactions?
leads.why: At the base fee seen in 1,024 consecutive blocks, 30,000,000 gas costs 0.018 dollars per block, and blocks arrive about every 0.54 seconds, which is under 3,000 dollars per day if the fee does not rise with use. Every exit from the PoolManager is a call to unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114) and would compete for that limit. If ordering is by arrival, or the fee is fixed, an ordinary account could hold liquidity providers out for as long as it pays. The stablecoin unit did not look at fee dynamics.

leads.question: Does the execution client of each of these OP Stack chains contain a rule that turns a user deposit into a failed deposit or leaves it out, as intercept_blacklisted_deposit does in the X Layer client? Search the handler and block executor of base/node, world-chain, celo-kona, mega-evm and the Conduit builds for calls made before a deposit executes.
leads.why: Forced inclusion through the L1 portal is the mitigation that every operator filtering finding on these chains relies on (F-017, F-030). On X Layer it turned out to be voidable at the execution layer. Soneium already restricts listed contracts at its RPC and sequencer and nobody read its execution client for the same rule.

leads.question: Do the B20 precompile on Base, the CAS20 dispatcher in the Jenner client and the Robinhood stock tokens have any path on which transfer returns true while the amount is credited to an account other than the named recipient or held by a guard contract, as TIP-20 does on Tempo for a recipient whose receive policy rejects the sender? Who names the account that can recover such funds?
leads.why: F-033 shows that on Tempo a payout can succeed for the PoolManager and never reach the recipient (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75 accepts a true word). OUSD exists on Base and on Tempo under the same policy administrator. If a recipient side policy on another chain can be set by a third party for a router or a wallet, payouts to it are diverted with no failed call to warn the user.

leads.question: Settle the two plausible HyperEVM items with one fact: when a treasury deployer names an EVM address as AQAv2 treasury, must that address sign a message, send a CoreWriter action or hold a HyperCore account first? Read the HyperCore action schema for the designation and look for a designation whose treasury address is a contract.
leads.why: F-020 and the new AQAv2 finding stay plausible on this point alone. If no consent is required, unsigned system transfers can move an ERC-20 balance out of a contract that never called transfer, which breaks assumption A2 for the PoolManager and changes the actor from operator to whoever can pass the stake and vote conditions.

leads.question: Settle F-024 with one fact: is the risk control filter of the block builder switched on for the X Layer mainnet sequencer, and has any source hash been written to the deposit blacklist at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727? An indexer with full log access for that contract answers the second part.
leads.why: F-024 is plausible because the filter state on mainnet is unknown, and the new high finding on voided deposits rests on source at one tag. Both verdicts depend on whether the rules are in use.

leads.question: Without comparing code, does the Unichain predeploy behave as src/PoolManager.sol says? With a caller contract placed by state override, check by eth_call: settle with value after sync of a token reverts with NonzeroNativeValue, settle after sync(address(0)) credits msg.value, a settle without payment credits zero, take reverts while locked, clear accepts only the exact positive delta, mint and burn move the delta and the claim by the same amount, and collectProtocolFees for a synced token reverts.
leads.why: Every Unichain clearance assumes src/ describes a contract of a different size that was placed at genesis. A behaviour test is the method the owner has not ruled out. A missing native value guard there would matter less than on Celo because ETH has no ERC-20 face on Unichain, yet the other checks cover the accounting of every pool on that chain.

leads.question: On Celo and Arc, read the deployed Universal Router and PositionManager: do they call sync(address(0)) before every native settle, do they ever treat the CELO token or 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 as the wrapped native currency, and what do they do with a route that names both address(0) and the token face of the same balance?
leads.why: The two chains are the only ones where the native asset has a transferable ERC-20 face, so they are where the guard at src/PoolManager.sol:356 and the comment at line 348 matter. The settlement model cleared core. The periphery that ordinary users go through was not read on either chain, and a router that settles the face with msg.value or skips the sync leaves its users with reverts or with funds credited to nobody.

leads.question: The Elysium bridge contract on HyperEVM holds 298,480 HYPE and executes child chain messages as calls made by itself. What happens when an Elysium account sends a message whose target is the HYPE bridge address 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222, a token system address or CoreWriter: is a HyperCore balance credited to the bridge contract, and can a later message spend it?
leads.why: The arbitrum-family unit left this open. The backing of every bridged asset on Elysium, including the HYPE and USDC that its PoolManager holds, sits in that contract. An ordinary Elysium account that can move the backing into a HyperCore account leaves holders of the bridged tokens, pools included, unable to withdraw to HyperEVM.

leads.question: Which go-ethereum commit do the sequencers of the three Nitro chains run (the endpoint reports nitro v3.13.0-rc.9 while the source was read at v3.11.3), and does EVM.Call in that commit keep the balance check for every caller, as the critic saw in OffchainLabs/go-ethereum master, where isSystemCall is used for witness gas only?
leads.why: The source reading of this unit is two releases behind the running build. Upstream go-ethereum now skips the value transfer for the system caller, and a merge of that change into Nitro would need a second look at which ArbOS paths use that caller.

leads.question: Is collect on the Arc fee controller (3,480 bytes at 0x2f2bd3f43880b9644211f16d861b0672aab23782) open to any caller, where does it send native USDC, and can the destination pay it back to the PoolManager inside the same transaction?
leads.why: collectProtocolFees exempts address(0) from the synced currency test with the remark that native settle uses msg.value (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). On Arc and Celo the native balance is also what balanceOf of the token face reports, so a native collection moves the figure that a pending settle of the face will read. The settlement model allowed a withdrawal at any point and found no gain. It did not model a destination that returns the funds.

leads.question: Where is the opcode fusion code of pull request 3395 in the BNB Smart Chain client that validators run, which opcode sequences does it fuse, and which sequences caused the bad block fixed by pull requests 3582 and 3584?
leads.why: The established L1 unit could not find the feature in the five files it read. An interpreter that rewrites bytecode has already produced one consensus fault on this chain, and the PoolManager bytecode is optimizer output with long stack sequences.

leads.question: After T14 activates on 2026-12-08, what does 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 answer to the PoolManager call shapes, and can an account of the new configurable type be the sender of a transaction whose address was fixed before its code or configuration existed?
leads.why: The address is codeless today and returns success to every call. Assumption A7 and the hook address rule depend on code at an address staying what it was, and a new account type is a new way for behaviour at a fixed address to change.

leads.question: From Blockscout or another indexer, what are the twenty largest token balances of the PoolManager on Soneium, Ink, Zora and World Chain, and which of them rebase, answer at a second address, or have a block list or pause role?
leads.why: The four chains have no L3 record of their own. The issuer finding F-028 lists three of them by analogy.

leads.question: In the parallel executors of Bor (BlockSTM), World Chain (flashblocks validation with block access lists) and Monad (optimistic execution with retries), is a transaction that is re-executed after a conflict always started with an empty transient map, and is the transient map of a discarded attempt ever merged into the state the next transaction reads?
leads.why: Three units cleared A1 from the serial path or from the per transaction state object and each noted that the merge step was not read to the end. The synced currency and reserves are the only PoolManager state that can outlive a call (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32), and a stale pair from a discarded attempt would be read by settle as real.
